summary: Earth has experienced five major mass extinctions, known as the 'Big Five', each caused by rapid climate changes or catastrophic events. These events are defined by the loss of at least 75% of species within a short geological period. Understanding them helps contextualize current extinction rates.

claims.text: There have been five mass extinctions in Earth's history, called the 'Big Five'.
claims.evidence_quote: There have been five big mass extinctions in Earth's history – these are called the 'Big Five'.

claims.text: A mass extinction is defined as at least 75% of species going extinct within a relatively short period, typically less than two million years.
claims.evidence_quote: In a mass extinction, at least 75% of species go extinct within a relatively (by geological standard) short period of time. Typically less than two million years.

claims.text: The End Ordovician extinction occurred 444 million years ago and caused the loss of 86% of species.
The Late Devonian extinction occurred 360 million years ago and caused the loss of 75% of species.
The End Permian extinction occurred 250 million years ago and caused the loss of 96% of species, the most severe of the Big Five.
The End Triassic extinction occurred 200 million years ago and caused the loss of 80% of species.
The End Cretaceous extinction occurred 65 million years ago and caused the loss of 76% of species, including the dinosaurs.
The End Permian extinction was caused by intense volcanic activity in Siberia, leading to global warming, ocean acidification, and acid rain.
claims.evidence_quote: Intense volcanic activity in Siberia. This caused global warming. Elevated CO2 and sulfur (H2S) levels from volcanoes caused ocean acidification, acid rain, and other changes in ocean and land chemistry.

claims.text: The End Cretaceous extinction was caused by an asteroid impact in Yucatán, Mexico, leading to a global cataclysm and rapid cooling.
claims.evidence_quote: Asteroid impact in Yucatán, Mexico. This caused a global cataclysm and rapid cooling.

claims.text: The End Ordovician extinction was caused by intense glacial and interglacial periods creating large sea-level swings and dramatic shoreline changes.
claims.evidence_quote: Intense glacial and interglacial periods created large sea-level swings and moved shorelines dramatically.

claims.text: The Late Devonian extinction was caused by rapid growth and diversification of land plants, leading to severe global cooling.
claims.evidence_quote: Rapid growth and diversification of land plants generated rapid and severe global cooling.

claims.text: The End Triassic extinction was caused by underwater volcanic activity in the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP), causing global warming and changes in ocean chemistry.
claims.evidence_quote: Underwater volcanic activity in the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) caused global warming and a dramatic change in the chemical composition of the oceans.

claims.text: The natural background extinction rate is about 10% of species lost every million years.
claims.evidence_quote: 10% of species are lost every million years

claims.text: We are currently far from a sixth mass extinction, but the trajectory depends on our actions.
claims.evidence_quote: Perhaps we are headed for a sixth mass extinction. But we are currently far from that point.
